twenty-forty in both eyes plus color recognition is only for CDL applicants.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F12","sec03-F14"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Basic is fifty, commercial is forty and colors.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Marcus sees with one eye and wants a basic license. Before you answer a single knowledge question or sit behind the wheel with an examiner, two gates come first. The first is paperwork: every applicant for a New Jersey driver license must have all the documents needed for the six-point ID Verification. The second is your eyesight, because every motorist must pass a vision screening. This lesson walks through both gates, explains the extra REAL ID model, compares the basic and commercial vision standards, and closes with what commercial drivers file and why you should tell the examiner about health problems.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Six points and REAL ID","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every applicant meets six-point ID Verification.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02"]},{"text":"REAL ID adds two address proofs.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02"]},{"text":"REAL ID adds one Social Security proof.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Start with the rule that covers everyone. Every applicant for a New Jersey driver license must bring all the documents needed to satisfy the six-point ID Verification. The rule names every applicant, whatever license they are after. If you want a REAL ID license or a REAL ID non-driver ID, the manual describes a two plus one plus six model. That means two proofs of your New Jersey address, one proof of your Social Security number, and documents that meet the six-point rule. So REAL ID does not replace the six points; it stacks the address and Social Security proofs on top of them.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Vision screening for everyone","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every motorist passes a vision screening.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},{"text":"Basic standard: twenty-fifty, lenses allowed.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},{"text":"One eye: same rule plus physician paperwork.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Every motorist must pass a vision screening, and the MVC has two tools when vision looks impaired: it may send the applicant to a physician, and it may periodically require a recheck. For a basic license, the standard is twenty-fifty vision, with or without corrective lenses, so glasses or contacts are fine. If you see with only one eye, you are not shut out. That one eye must meet the same twenty-fifty rule, and you must bring documentation signed by a licensed physician. Keep the structure in mind: one standard for basic drivers, and the one-eye case simply applies that standard to the eye you see with.","fact_ids":["sec03-F03","sec03-F12","sec03-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Basic versus CDL vision","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F12","sec03-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Basic license: twenty-fifty.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F12","sec03-F14"]},{"text":"CDL: twenty-forty in both eyes.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F12","sec03-F14"]},{"text":"CDL: tell red, green and amber apart.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F12","sec03-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is where learners mix things up. The manual gives two vision standards side by side. Basic license applicants need twenty-fifty vision, with or without corrective lenses. CDL applicants face a tighter rule: twenty-forty vision in both eyes, still with or without corrective lenses, and they must be able to tell red, green and amber lights apart. So the commercial standard is stricter on sharpness, applies to both eyes, and adds color recognition. When a question mentions a commercial driver, reach for twenty-forty and colors. When it mentions an ordinary car license, the number is twenty-fifty.","fact_ids":["sec03-R01","sec03-F12","sec03-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"CDL paperwork and your health","fact_ids":["sec03-R02","sec03-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Commercial drivers file a Self-Certification form.","fact_ids":["sec03-R02","sec03-F16"]},{"text":"Medical examiner's certificate, if applicable.","fact_ids":["sec03-R02","sec03-F16"]},{"text":"Tell the examiner about health problems.","fact_ids":["sec03-R02","sec03-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Commercial drivers carry one more paperwork duty. Federal law and New Jersey rules require them to file a CDL Holder Self-Certification form and, if applicable, a medical examiner's certificate completed by a federally certified medical examiner. That certificate must come from a federally certified examiner, not just any doctor. For every applicant, commercial or not, there is also an honesty rule about health. Applicants must tell the examiner about health problems, and a medical review may be necessary. Hiding a condition is not an option the manual allows; telling the examiner is the expected first step, and a review may follow.","fact_ids":["sec03-R02","sec03-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the one-eye rule","fact_ids":["sec03-F13","sec03-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"One seeing eye, basic license.","fact_ids":["sec03-F13","sec03-F12"]},{"text":"Which standard and which paperwork?","fact_ids":["sec03-F13","sec03-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Marcus sees with only one eye and wants an ordinary basic license. Which vision standard must that eye meet, and what paperwork does he bring? Work it out before reading on. The answer is that his seeing eye must meet the twenty-fifty rule, the same standard every basic license applicant meets, and he must bring documentation signed by a licensed physician. He does not need the twenty-forty commercial standard, because he is not applying for a CDL. The one-eye rule is not a separate number; it borrows the basic twenty-fifty standard and adds the physician's signed paperwork.","fact_ids":["sec03-F13","sec03-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Your first two gates","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-F14","sec03-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Six points for everyone; REAL ID adds more.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-F14","sec03-F16"]},{"text":"Basic twenty-fifty; CDL twenty-forty and colors.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-F14","sec03-F16"]},{"text":"Report health problems to the examiner.","fact_ids":["sec03-F01","sec03-F02","sec03-F12","sec03-F13","sec03-F14","sec03-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us pull this lesson together. Then we cover who the test is built for: the many languages it is offered in, the oral version for applicants who cannot read, and the rules for using an interpreter. Interpreters come in two kinds in the manual, foreign-language and deaf or hard of hearing, and each has its own approval route and its own steps. By the end you will know which path fits which applicant.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What the test contains","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Regular questions plus an organ donation survey.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Passing depends on the share answered correctly.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05"]},{"text":"Many languages, including American Sign Language.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"The knowledge test has its set of regular questions, and the manual notes one extra item: a survey question about organ donation. The test is offered in English and American Sign Language, and also in Albanian, Arabic, Chinese, French, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish and Turkish. Anyone who needs an interpreter must also tell the MVC at least two weeks before the planned date of the written knowledge test, so the request has to be made well ahead.","fact_ids":["sec03-F06","sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Offered language or interpreter","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F05","sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"American Sign Language is on the list.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F05","sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},{"text":"Unlisted language: failed attempt first.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F05","sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},{"text":"Then at least two weeks' notice.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F05","sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. American Sign Language is already on the knowledge test language list, so it is an offered language. A state-approved interpreter for a language that is not listed is arranged only after a failed attempt in an offered language and with at least two weeks' notice to the MVC. So the order is fixed: check the list, try an offered language, give notice, and only then expect an interpreter. Skipping the attempt or the notice breaks the sequence.","fact_ids":["sec03-R03","sec03-F05","sec03-F07","sec03-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Who counts as approved","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F09","sec03-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Foreign-language: courts' Registry of Interpreters.","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F09","sec03-R04"]},{"text":"Deaf: national certification or Division approval.","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F09","sec03-R04"]},{"text":"MVC pays deaf interpreter fees after voucher.","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F09","sec03-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Approval works differently for each kind of interpreter. An approved foreign-language interpreter is someone listed on the Registry of Interpreters and Agencies kept by the NJ Administrative Office of the Courts, Language Services Section. An approved deaf or hard of hearing interpreter either holds certification from the National Registry of Interpreters for the Deaf and is on file with the NJ Division of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing, or has been evaluated by that Division and placed on its approved list. For Deaf or Hard of Hearing applicants, the MVC provides approved interpreters and pays the knowledge-test interpreter fees once a completed payment voucher form is submitted.","fact_ids":["sec03-F10","sec03-F11","sec03-F09","sec03-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the interpreter steps","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Native language not offered.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-R03"]},{"text":"What must happen first?","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: Tomas's native language is not on the knowledge test list, and he wants a state-approved interpreter. What two things must happen before one is arranged? Work it out before reading on. Second, he must tell the MVC at least two weeks before the planned date of the written knowledge test. With both steps done, the interpreter can be arranged. Notice that he cannot skip straight to an interpreter, and he cannot give notice on the morning of the test.","fact_ids":["sec03-F07","sec03-F08","sec03-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Knowledge test recap","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05","sec03-F06","sec03-R03","sec03-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Survey question; pass by share correct.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05","sec03-F06","sec03-R03","sec03-R04"]},{"text":"Many languages, oral option, interpreters.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05","sec03-F06","sec03-R03","sec03-R04"]},{"text":"MVC calls once an interpreter is secured.","fact_ids":["sec03-F04","sec03-F15","sec03-F05","sec03-F06","sec03-R03","sec03-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us wrap up. What license does she get?","fact_ids":["sec03-F19","sec03-R05"]},"answer":{"text":"A probationary license for one year, and she must follow New Jersey's GDL rules.","fact_ids":["sec03-F19"]},"rationale":{"text":"The four-year basic license is for transfers aged eighteen or older; the seventeen-to-eighteen group gets the probationary path.","fact_ids":["sec03-R05"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Bringing a license with you","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]},"lines":[{"text":"Out-of-state adults, out-of-state teens.","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]},{"text":"Out-of-country applicants test.","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]}],"narration":{"text":"Many New Jersey applicants already drive somewhere else. This lesson sorts them into three groups. First are adults with a valid, non-provisional license from another state or a listed territory, who may have the knowledge and road tests waived. Second are younger transfers, aged seventeen to eighteen, who follow a probationary path under New Jersey's GDL rules. Third are applicants from outside the country, who must test. For each group we will cover what is waived, what still has to be submitted, and which license comes out at the end. Watch the ages and the word non-provisional, because they decide which group you are in.","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The adult transfer","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"Eighteen or older, valid, non-provisional.","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Tests may be waived.","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Six-point ID, four-year license, surrender.","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"Knowledge and road tests may be waived for transfer applicants aged eighteen or older who hold a valid, non-provisional license from any of the fifty states, the District of Columbia, Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico or the US Virgin Islands. All three conditions matter: the age, a valid license, and non-provisional status. A waiver of the tests does not mean a waiver of the paperwork. Transfer applicants still submit the six-point ID documents. In return they receive a four-year basic New Jersey license, and they must surrender the out-of-state license, so you do not keep both cards.","fact_ids":["sec03-F17","sec03-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Adult versus teen transfer","fact_ids":["sec03-R05","sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"Eighteen or older: four-year basic license.","fact_ids":["sec03-R05","sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Seventeen to eighteen: one-year probationary license.","fact_ids":["sec03-R05","sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F18"]},{"text":"Teens follow GDL rules.","fact_ids":["sec03-R05","sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"This contrast trips people up. Two transfer applicants can both hold a valid license and still leave with different New Jersey licenses. A transfer applicant aged eighteen or older with a valid non-provisional license gets a four-year basic license. An out-of-state applicant aged seventeen to eighteen with a valid license receives a probationary license for one year and must follow New Jersey's GDL rules. So age decides the outcome, not just whether the old license is valid. When a question gives you a seventeen-year-old newcomer, think probationary and GDL; when it gives you an adult, think four-year basic license.","fact_ids":["sec03-R05","sec03-F17","sec03-F19","sec03-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec03-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Coming from another country","fact_ids":["sec03-F20","sec03-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Must pass knowledge test and vision screening.","fact_ids":["sec03-F20","sec03-R06"]},{"text":"A road test may also be required.","fact_ids":["sec03-F20","sec03-R06"]},{"text":"Results stay valid for two years.","fact_ids":["sec03-F20","sec03-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Applicants from outside the United States follow a different rule.
